prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realization at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B015 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. The criterion I apply is the one I have stated publicly, a discovery or invention with an identifiable origin and a demonstrated payoff. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is the origin, because it removes the trapping-light shift while confining many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime. Ye's group is the demonstration, because it took strontium lattice clocks to roughly 1e-18 and showed what a many-atom architecture delivers, including millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. Independent reproduction at several laboratories makes the performance claim a matter of international comparison and not of one group's say-so. The round-1 exchange has strengthened my view of two points. First, the chair's question about wording has a workable answer: the citation should name the invention of the lattice clock and its realization at the 1e-18 level, and should not mention frequency metrology generally, so that it is plainly distinct from the 2005 comb prize (which made optical frequencies countable) and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems. Second, the objections raised against B015 concern framing and credit boundaries, and none of them touches the core claim. A single-part, two-name prize is also the cleanest configuration on the shortlist, since it needs no truncation under the three-laureate limit.
statement.case_against: The reservations I carried into round 1 remain, and I weigh them as follows. The SI redefinition of the second has not happened; I treat that as a supporting consideration and not as a precondition, because the performance of lattice clocks is already established by independent comparison and the prize is for the invention and its realization, not for the redefinition. The neighbouring 2005 and 2012 prizes are a real constraint on wording, and if the committee cannot agree a citation that separates them, that would be a serious problem. The credit boundary is the weakest point: the Paris (Lemonde, Le Targat), PTB and NIST lattice work, Ludlow and Lemke, and the single-ion community reached comparable uncertainties by other routes, and I cannot verify from the supplied material how the committee should divide inventor from refiner. My own working line is that the concept (Katori) and the first demonstration of the performance breakthrough (Ye) are the two contributions the others built on or confirmed. Finally, the result is a measurement capability and not a new phenomenon, which is why Danielsson's objection deserves a direct answer and not a dismissal.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B006 as his first choice, a prediction followed by an unexpected experimental result, and asks of B015 what the lattice clock has taught us about nature and not only how precisely it measures; he regards the fundamental-physics payoff as still prospective.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection to B015 and I do not think it should be waved away. My answer is that the clock is both an invention and an instrument that has already produced measurements of nature: the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a single atomic sample and clock comparisons that constrain variation of constants are results of this type, though they are not yet discoveries on the scale of a new phase of matter. I would not claim more than that, and the citation should not either. On B006 I remain where I was: I rank it third and it is my first alternative. The magic angle was predicted and nature responded with correlated and superconducting states, which is what you say you look for. But the mechanism is unresolved, the Cao et al. experimental team falls outside the supplied credit, and I would not want us to write a citation that has to be retracted. Your own point that the discovery of the phases does not depend on the mechanism is fair. If the committee sees it that way, I would not obstruct B006 in a later year, but I do not find that it beats B015 on maturity and credit now.

responses.point: Kroll holds B015 first, regards the Katori and Ye credit as the cleanest on the shortlist, and asks whether a two-part prize, for example B015 with B006, is worth considering given the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I considered a two-part configuration seriously and I do not support it. Pairing B015 with B006 would leave one part with a single person or force Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero or MacDonald out of a three-name credit, and the second part would carry the unresolved interpretation problem that is my reason for not putting B006 first. Adding B013 is no better: its support is concentrated, and I should not be the deciding voice on my own field. A prize for the lattice clock alone is a complete, defensible statement. I also agree with Kroll's earlier qualification, which I take on board: Ye's many-body and redshift results should be read as demonstrations of what Katori's concept made possible, not as a separate discovery, and the Hall laboratory stay he discloses does not touch Katori or Ye, so I see no reason for him to step back.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first, argues that a reader of the 2005 comb citation would see the lattice clock as a distinct step, and raises the single-ion clock lineage and the early Paris and PTB/NIST lattice work as the edge of the credit.
responses.response: I agree with the comb distinction and would use it nearly as she puts it: the comb made optical frequencies countable and the lattice clock is what is counted with them. I would go one step further than her text and keep the 1e-18 level in the citation, because it states what is new relative to 2012 (neutral atoms in a many-atom lattice, not a single ion). Her citation omits that level and I would ask her to accept it. On the single-ion lineage, I think a narrowly worded lattice-clock citation is honest and not exclusionary, since the prize would honour a specific architecture and not the whole of optical clocks. If she or the committee wants ion and lattice clocks treated together, I think that reopens attribution in a way the supplied names cannot settle, and that is a reason to keep the citation narrow.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B055, argues that it is a mature organizing principle with two decades of confirmation, and states that in his view it does not exceed B055 in reach, though he would not oppose B015 if the committee wants the cleanest credit.
responses.response: I take the maturity and conceptual reach of B055 seriously, and I note that he has moved B015 from last to a second alternative and says he would not oppose it. His own account of B055's weak point is the credit: Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy and the ARPES work are outside the three supplied names, and the experimental realization depended on a theoretical proposal that falls outside them too. That is the same attribution burden that I am asked to bear for B015, but at larger scale, so I weigh the two differently on exact credit. I do not regard scientific reach as something that an enabling invention must match to be prize-worthy, since the criterion is discovery or invention. I would ask him what specific citation wording he thinks would defend the three names to the public; if there is a convincing answer I would reconsider B055 as a later-year candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree a citation that clearly separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I would accept the 1e-18 wording but cannot guarantee that colleagues will.

Whether crediting only Katori and Ye is defensible against the Paris, PTB, NIST and single-ion contributions; I rely on my recollection of the clock literature and have not verified priority or record uncertainties.
How much weight the pending SI redefinition of the second should carry; I treat it as supporting evidence and not as a precondition.
Whether Danielsson's distinction between a measurement advance and a discovery of new phenomena will carry weight with colleagues who have not yet stated a view in this round.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene should be held for a later year because of the unresolved pairing mechanism or judged mature enough because the discovery of the phases does not depend on it.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. B013 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my own field of transmission electron microscopy; I have no documented personal connection to Rose, Urban or Haider, but I should not be the deciding voice on it and I will abstain from advocating it. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague; his interest in B024 does not involve my work and has no effect on B015, and I have no view on whether he should recuse beyond noting that the matter belongs to him and the chair. I record no documented tie to Katori, Ye, Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero. My public remark that the prize is for a discovery or invention and not for lifetime achievement, as reported by Tohoku University and not from a transcript, is the standard I have applied, and my 2023 service as Chair confers no special authority on these questions.
